title: FET Circuits
description: JFETs and MOSFETs in practice: square law, transconductance, followers, current sources, analog switches and power switching.

study.title: The FET family
study.body: A FET's drain current is set by the gate–source voltage $V_{GS}$; the gate draws essentially no dc current. **JFETs** and **depletion** MOSFETs conduct at $V_{GS}$ = 0 and need reverse gate voltage to turn off. **Enhancement** MOSFETs (almost all MOSFETs you buy) are off at $V_{GS}$ = 0 and conduct beyond the threshold $V_T$. A JFET gate is a pn junction: keep it reverse biased. For p-channel parts every polarity is reversed.

study.title: Explore: ohmic and saturation regions
study.body: At small $V_{DS}$ the channel is a resistor $R_{DS} \approx 1/[2k(V_{GS}-V_T)]$ (the **linear** or ohmic region), so a FET is a voltage-controlled resistor. Beyond $V_{DS} = V_{GS} - V_T$ the channel pinches off and the current hardly depends on $V_{DS}$ (**saturation**, the current-source region). For a JFET use $V_T = V_P$ (pinch-off) and $k = I_{DSS}/V_P^2$. The graph: $k$ = 0.5 mA/V², $V_T$ = 2 V.

study.title: Explore: transconductance
study.body: In saturation $g_m = \Delta I_D/\Delta V_{GS}$ grows only as $\sqrt{I_D}$, while a BJT has $g_m = I_C/(25\text{ mV})$. At 1 mA a small-signal FET has only about 0.5–3 mS, against 40 mS for a BJT; at very low currents it approaches $I_D/(40\ldots60\text{ mV})$ at best. So FETs are chosen for their zero gate current, not for their gain.

study.title: Common-source amplifier and source follower
study.body: Output at the drain: a **common-source** amplifier with gain $-g_mR_D$ (source bypassed), or $-g_mR_D/(1+g_mR_S)$ with an unbypassed $R_S$ (≈ $-R_D/R_S$ if $g_mR_S \gg 1$). Output at the source: a **source follower** with gain somewhat below 1 and output resistance $1/g_m \parallel R_S$. With $g_m$ = 2 mS that is about 500 Ω, versus 25 Ω for an emitter follower at 1 mA.

study.title: JFET current sources and self-bias
study.body: With gate tied to source a JFET passes about $I_{DSS}$ as long as $V_{DS}$ exceeds $|V_P|$: a two-terminal current source. A source resistor lowers the current, because $V_{GS} = -I_DR_S$ becomes negative; the same trick self-biases a JFET amplifier with one gate resistor to ground. $I_{DSS}$ varies by up to a factor 5 between parts of one type, and $V_P$ by several volts, so trim $R_S$ (or use an op-amp current source) when accuracy matters. ($J_1$ is an n-channel JFET.)

study.title: Analog switches
study.body: A MOSFET in the ohmic region passes signals both ways. A single NMOS conducts badly when the signal approaches its gate drive, so CMOS switches put an NMOS and a PMOS in parallel with opposite gate signals (a **transmission gate**): $R_{ON}$ stays low (5–100 Ω) over the whole supply range. Limits: signals must stay within the rails, $R_{ON}$ and the load capacitance form a low-pass, and at turn-off the gate edge dumps a charge $Q_{inj}$ (a few pC) into the load. A multiplexer is a set of such switches plus a decoder.

study.title: MOSFET as a power switch
study.body: Low-side switch: load from $V_{DD}$ to the drain, source to ground. Use a **logic-level** MOSFET whose $R_{DS(on)}$ is specified at the gate voltage you have ($V_{GS(th)}$ is only where conduction begins); conduction loss is $I_D^2R_{DS(on)}$. The driver must deliver the gate charge $Q_g$: $t_{sw} \approx Q_g/I_G$, and each edge costs switching loss. Inductive loads need a flyback diode, otherwise the drain flies up until the MOSFET avalanches (its built-in source–drain body diode does not help here).

steps.title: Voltage-controlled devices
steps.body: A FET is controlled by $V_{GS}$, not by an input current: the MOSFET gate is insulated by oxide, the JFET gate is a reverse-biased junction (pA–nA leakage). FETs come as n- or p-channel, and as **depletion** types (conducting at $V_{GS}$ = 0: all JFETs and depletion MOSFETs) or **enhancement** types (off at $V_{GS}$ = 0). The graph shows the transfer curves of three n-channel parts.

steps.prompt: Match each device to its gate behaviour.
pairs: On at 0 V; gate junction must stay reverse biased
Off at 0 V; on for $V_{GS} > V_T > 0$
Off at 0 V; on for $V_{GS} < V_T < 0$
On at 0 V; gate may swing either way
steps.explanation: Depletion devices (JFETs, depletion MOSFETs) have a channel at $V_{GS}$ = 0; enhancement MOSFETs need $|V_{GS}| > |V_T|$ to create one. The insulated gate of a depletion MOSFET may go positive or negative, while a JFET gate must stay reverse biased (forward bias above about 0.5 V makes the gate conduct). p-channel parts use the opposite polarities.

steps.prompt: Which transfer curve belongs to a **p-channel enhancement** MOSFET? (Horizontal axis $V_{GS}$, vertical line at $V_{GS}$ = 0, vertical axis $|I_D|$.)
steps.explanation: Enhancement means no current at $V_{GS}$ = 0; p-channel means the gate must go **negative** beyond $V_T$ (here about −1.5 V). The curve starting at +1.5 V is the n-channel enhancement MOSFET. The two curves that conduct at $V_{GS}$ = 0 are JFETs: the n-JFET turns off for negative, the p-JFET for positive gate voltages.

steps.title: Explore: two regions
steps.body: Drag $V_{GS}$. Left of the dashed boundary is the ohmic region: near the origin the curve is almost a straight line, so the FET acts as a resistor whose value is set by $V_{GS}$ (it bends over as $V_{DS}$ approaches $V_{GS}-V_T$). Right of the boundary the current is flat: the FET is a current source with $I_D = k(V_{GS}-V_T)^2$. Here $k$ = 0.5 mA/V² and $V_T$ = 2 V.

steps.prompt: An n-channel MOSFET has $k$ = {{k*1000}} mA/V² and $V_T$ = {{VT|V}}. Find $I_D$ at $V_{GS}$ = {{VGS|V}} and $V_{DS}$ = 10 V.
steps.explanation:
$V_{DS}$ = 10 V is larger than $V_{GS}-V_T$ = {{VGS-VT|V}}, so the FET is in saturation:
$I_D = k(V_{GS}-V_T)^2$ = {{k*1000}} mA/V² × ({{VGS-VT|V}})² = {{k*(VGS-VT)^2|A}}.

steps.prompt: An n-channel MOSFET with $V_T$ = {{VT|V}} has $V_{GS}$ = {{VGS|V}} and $V_{DS}$ = {{VDS|V}}. It operates in saturation (the current-source region).
steps.explanation: Saturation needs $V_{DS} > V_{GS}-V_T$ = {{VGS|V}} − {{VT|V}} = {{VGS-VT|V}}. Here $V_{DS}$ = {{VDS|V}}. If $V_{DS}$ is smaller, the channel is not pinched off and the FET behaves as a resistor (ohmic region), as in a switch that is fully on.

steps.title: Transconductance
steps.body: The small-signal gain of a FET is its transconductance $g_m = \Delta I_D/\Delta V_{GS}$. Differentiating the square law gives the formulas below. Compare a BJT: $g_m = I_C/25$ mV. At 1 mA a BJT has 40 mS; a FET with $V_{GS}-V_T$ = 1 V has only $2 \cdot 1\text{ mA}/1\text{ V}$ = 2 mS.

steps.prompt: A MOSFET runs at $I_D$ = {{ID|A}} with $V_{GS}-V_T$ = {{Vov|V}}.

ask.prompt: How many times larger is the $g_m$ of a BJT at the same current?
ask.explanation:
BJT: $g_m = I_C/25\text{ mV}$ = {{ID/0.025|S}}. FET: $2I_D/(V_{GS}-V_T)$ = {{2*ID/Vov|S}}.
Ratio: $\frac{V_{GS}-V_T}{2 \times 25\text{ mV}}$ = {{Vov/0.05}}.

steps.prompt: Doubling the drain current of a MOSFET in saturation doubles its transconductance.
steps.explanation: $g_m = 2\sqrt{kI_D}$, so doubling $I_D$ raises $g_m$ by only $\sqrt{2}$ ≈ 1.41. (A BJT's $g_m = I_C/25$ mV does double.)

steps.prompt: When is a FET input stage clearly the better choice than a BJT?
options: The source has 10 MΩ internal resistance
You need the most voltage gain per milliamp
You need the lowest possible offset voltage
A follower must have the lowest output resistance
steps.explanation: A FET draws (almost) no gate current, so a 10 MΩ source sees no loading or bias-current error. For gain, low offset and low follower output resistance ($1/g_m$) a BJT wins, because its $g_m$ is much higher and its $V_{BE}$ is better matched.

steps.prompt: The common-source amplifier is biased at $I_D$ = {{ID|A}}; the MOSFET has $k$ = {{k*1000}} mA/V². $C_S$ bypasses $R_S$ for signals.

ask.explanation:
$g_m = 2\sqrt{kI_D}$ = {{gm|S}}.
$A_v = -g_mR_D$ = −{{gm|S}} × {{RD|Ω}} = {{-gm*RD}}. A BJT with $g_m = I_C/25$ mV would give {{-ID/0.025*RD}}.

ask.prompt: $C_S$ is removed, so $R_S$ is no longer bypassed. Find the new gain (with sign).
ask.explanation:
$g_m$ = {{gm|S}}. The source resistor gives local feedback:
$A_v = -\frac{g_mR_D}{1+g_mR_S}$ = −{{gm*RD}}/(1 + {{gm*RS}}) = {{-gm*RD/(1+gm*RS)}}. Less gain, but less dependent on $g_m$.

steps.prompt: A source follower is biased where $g_m$ = {{gm|S}}; $R_S$ = {{RS|Ω}}.

ask.explanation: $A_v = \frac{g_mR_S}{1+g_mR_S}$ = {{gm*RS}}/(1 + {{gm*RS}}) = {{gm*RS/(1+gm*RS)||4}}. A FET follower loses noticeably more than an emitter follower.

Looking into the source you see $1/g_m$ = {{1/gm|Ω}}, in parallel with $R_S$:
$R_{out} = \frac{1}{g_m}\parallel R_S$ = {{par(1/gm, RS)|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: An n-JFET has $I_{DSS}$ = {{IDSS|A}} and $V_P$ = {{VP|V}}. Which $R_S$ makes this current sink carry {{I|A}}?
steps.explanation:
Solve the square law for $V_{GS}$: $V_{GS} = V_P\left(1-\sqrt{I_D/I_{DSS}}\right)$ = {{VP|V}} × (1 − √{{I/IDSS||3}}) = {{VGS|V}}.
The gate is at the bottom of $R_S$, so $V_{GS} = -I_DR_S$: $R_S = -V_{GS}/I_D$ = {{-VGS|V}}/{{I|A}} = {{RSt|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: Self-bias of a JFET ($I_{DSS}$ = {{IDSS|A}}, $V_P$ = {{VP|V}}). Set $R_S$ so the bias line $I_D = -V_{GS}/R_S$ crosses the transfer curve at $I_D$ = {{I|A}} (green point).
steps.explanation: At $I_D$ = {{I|A}} the transfer curve gives $V_{GS} = V_P(1-\sqrt{I_D/I_{DSS}})$ = {{VGSt|V}}. The bias line must pass through that point: $R_S = -V_{GS}/I_D$ = {{RSt|Ω}}. A larger $R_S$ makes the line flatter and the current smaller.

steps.prompt: A MOSFET with $k$ = {{k*1000}} mA/V² and $V_T$ = {{VT|V}} is used at small $V_{DS}$ as a voltage-controlled resistor.

ask.explanation: In the ohmic region near $V_{DS}$ = 0: $R_{DS} = \frac{1}{2k(V_{GS}-V_T)}$ = 1/(2 × {{k*1000}} mA/V² × {{VGS-VT|V}}) = {{1/(2*k*(VGS-VT))|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: A JFET datasheet gives $g_m$ = {{gm0|S}} at $V_{GS}$ = 0 ($I_D = I_{DSS}$ = {{IDSS|A}}). You bias it halfway to pinch-off, $V_{GS} = V_P/2$.

ask.explanation: $g_m = 2k(V_{GS}-V_P)$ is proportional to the distance from pinch-off. Halfway there it is half the datasheet value: {{gm0/2|S}}.

steps.prompt: A JFET source follower and an emitter follower both run at 1 mA. The JFET has $g_m$ = 2 mS. Their output resistances (ignoring $R_S$, $R_E$ and the source resistance) are about:
steps.explanation: A follower's output resistance is $1/g_m$. JFET: 1/2 mS = 500 Ω. BJT: $g_m$ = 1 mA/25 mV = 40 mS, so 25 Ω. The BJT follower is about 20 times stiffer, unless the source resistance is so high that its $R_s/\beta$ term dominates.

steps.prompt: A JFET current source (gate tied to source) keeps its current constant even when its drain–source voltage drops to 0.2 V.
steps.explanation: With $V_{GS}$ = 0 it stays in saturation only while $V_{DS} > V_{GS}-V_P = |V_P|$ (typically 1–5 V). At 0.2 V it is in the ohmic region and acts as a resistor, so the current falls. Every current source needs some 'compliance' voltage.

steps.prompt: When an analog switch opens, it injects $Q_{inj}$ = {{Q|C}} into the hold capacitor $C_H$.

ask.prompt: With $C_H$ = {{CH|F}}, how big is the step (pedestal) in the held voltage?
ask.explanation: $\Delta V = \frac{Q_{inj}}{C_H}$ = {{Q|C}} / {{CH|F}} = {{Q/CH|V}}.

ask.prompt: What is the smallest $C_H$ that keeps the step below {{dV|V}}?
ask.explanation: $C_H \ge \frac{Q_{inj}}{\Delta V}$ = {{Q|C}} / {{dV|V}} = {{Q/dV|F}}. A bigger capacitor reduces the glitch but makes the switch slower to follow the signal ($\tau = R_{ON}C_H$).

steps.prompt: A switch with $R_{ON}$ = {{Ron|Ω}} charges a hold capacitor $C_H$ = {{CH|F}} from a stiff source.

ask.explanation: $\tau = R_{ON}C_H$ = {{Ron|Ω}} × {{CH|F}} = {{Ron*CH|s}}.

ask.prompt: How long must the switch stay closed to settle within 0.1 % of a full-scale step?
ask.explanation: The error decays as $e^{-t/\tau}$; 0.1 % needs $t = \tau\ln(1000) \approx 6.9\tau$ = 6.9 × {{Ron*CH|s}} = {{Ron*CH*ln(1000)|s}}.

steps.prompt: Why does a CMOS analog switch use an NMOS and a PMOS in parallel?
options: Each alone has a high $R_{ON}$ near one rail; together $R_{ON}$ stays low over the whole range
So it can pass signals beyond the supply rails
steps.explanation: The NMOS needs $V_{GS} = V_{DD} - v_{signal}$ well above $V_T$, so it fails near the positive rail; the PMOS fails near the negative rail. In parallel one of them always conducts well, so the transmission gate has a fairly flat $R_{ON}$. The signal must still stay between the rails, or the drain–body junctions conduct.

steps.prompt: A MOSFET switch carries a dc current of {{I|A}}. Its $R_{DS(on)}$ = {{Rds|Ω}} at 25 °C.

ask.prompt: When hot, $R_{DS(on)}$ rises by about 50 %. Find the conduction loss then.
ask.explanation: $P = I^2 \times 1.5R_{DS(on)}$ = ({{I|A}})² × {{1.5*Rds|Ω}} = {{1.5*I^2*Rds|W}}. Always use the hot value from the datasheet curve when sizing the heatsink.

steps.prompt: A power MOSFET has a total gate charge $Q_g$ = {{Qg|C}}. The gate driver supplies {{IG|A}}. Estimate the switching time.
steps.explanation: $t_{sw} \approx \frac{Q_g}{I_G}$ = {{Qg|C}} / {{IG|A}} = {{Qg/IG|s}}. A microcontroller pin (≈ 20 mA) is slow for large MOSFETs; a gate driver delivering amperes switches in tens of ns.

steps.prompt: A MOSFET switches {{I|A}} at {{V|V}} with $t_r = t_f$ = {{tsw|s}} at $f$ = {{f|Hz}}. Estimate the switching loss.
steps.explanation:
During each edge voltage and current overlap; the estimate is
$P_{sw} \approx \tfrac{1}{2}V I(t_r+t_f)f$ = 0.5 × {{V|V}} × {{I|A}} × {{2*tsw|s}} × {{f|Hz}} = {{V*I*tsw*f|W}}.
It grows with frequency, so fast gate drive matters at high PWM rates.

steps.prompt: Tap the component that protects $Q_1$ when it switches off the inductive load.
steps.explanation: When $Q_1$ turns off, the load inductance keeps its current flowing ($v = L\,di/dt$). Without $D_1$ the drain would fly up until the MOSFET breaks down. $D_1$ gives the current a path back to $V_{DD}$, clamping the drain at $V_{DD}$ + 0.7 V. $R_G$ limits the gate current and damps ringing; $R_{GS}$ keeps the MOSFET off when the logic pin floats (e.g. during reset).

steps.prompt: Match each datasheet parameter to what it tells you.
pairs: Driver current needed for fast switching
Where the MOSFET just starts to conduct
steps.explanation: $R_{DS(on)}$ is only meaningful at the stated $V_{GS}$; at $V_{GS(th)}$ the current is just a few hundred µA, so the threshold says nothing about being fully on. $Q_g$ divided by the gate current gives the switching time. Choose $V_{DSS}$ with margin above the supply plus any inductive spikes.

steps.prompt: A MOSFET with $V_{GS(th)}$ = 2 V is fully on when driven from a 3.3 V logic pin.
steps.explanation: At threshold the MOSFET barely conducts. Check that $R_{DS(on)}$ is specified at $V_{GS}$ = 2.5 V or 3.3 V (a 'logic-level' or 'low-threshold' part). A standard MOSFET is specified at 10 V and may still have a large $R_{DS(on)}$ at 3.3 V.

steps.prompt: Design a MOSFET source follower: the gate sits at {{VG|V}} (set by a divider), $k$ = {{k*1000}} mA/V², $V_T$ = {{VT|V}}, and the bias current must be {{ID|A}}.

ask.explanation:
$V_{GS} = V_T + \sqrt{I_D/k}$ = {{VGS|V}}, so the source sits at $V_S = V_G - V_{GS}$ = {{VG-VGS|V}}.
$R_S = V_S/I_D$ = {{VG-VGS|V}} / {{ID|A}} = {{RSd|Ω}}.

ask.prompt: Find the output resistance at the source.
ask.explanation: $g_m = 2\sqrt{kI_D}$ = {{gm|S}}, so $1/g_m$ = {{1/gm|Ω}}. With $R_S = (V_G - V_{GS})/I_D$ = {{RSd|Ω}} in parallel: $R_{out}$ = {{par(1/gm, RSd)|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: A PWM motor drive switches {{I|A}} from {{V|V}} (freewheeling diode across the motor). The MOSFET has $R_{DS(on)}$ = {{Rds|Ω}} (hot), $t_r = t_f$ = {{tsw|s}}, duty cycle $D$ = {{D}}, $f$ = {{f|Hz}}.

ask.explanation: The MOSFET conducts a fraction $D$ of the time: $P_{cond} = DI^2R_{DS(on)}$ = {{D}} × ({{I|A}})² × {{Rds|Ω}} = {{Pc|W}}.
$P_{cond} = DI^2R_{DS(on)}$ = {{Pc|W}} and $P_{sw} \approx \tfrac12 VI(t_r+t_f)f$ = {{Ps|W}}. Total: {{Pc+Ps|W}}.

ask.prompt: At what PWM frequency would the switching loss equal the conduction loss?
ask.explanation:
$P_{sw}$ is proportional to $f$: $VI t_{sw} f = DI^2R_{DS(on)}$ gives
$f = \frac{DIR_{DS(on)}}{Vt_{sw}}$ = {{Pc|W}} / ({{V|V}} × {{I|A}} × {{tsw|s}}) = {{Pc/(V*I*tsw)|Hz}}.

steps.prompt: A gate driver swings 0 to {{Vdr|V}} through $R_G$ = {{RG|Ω}}. During switching the gate sits at the plateau voltage {{Vpl|V}}; $Q_g$ = {{Qg|C}}.

ask.prompt: Find the gate current during the plateau (turn-on).
ask.explanation: $I_G = \frac{V_{drive} - V_{plateau}}{R_G}$ = ({{Vdr|V}} − {{Vpl|V}}) / {{RG|Ω}} = {{IG|A}}.

$I_G = (V_{drive}-V_{plateau})/R_G$ = {{IG|A}}, so $t \approx Q_g/I_G$ = {{Qg|C}} / {{IG|A}} = {{Qg/IG|s}}. At turn-off the driver pulls the gate to 0 V and the current is only $V_{plateau}/R_G$ = {{Vpl/RG|A}}, so turn-off takes about {{Qg*RG/Vpl|s}}.

steps.prompt: A sample-and-hold uses a switch with $Q_{inj}$ = {{Q|C}} and $R_{ON}$ = {{Ron|Ω}}. The pedestal must stay below {{dV|V}}.

ask.explanation: $C_H \ge Q_{inj}/\Delta V$ = {{Q|C}} / {{dV|V}} = {{Cmin|F}}.

ask.prompt: With that capacitor, how long must the switch stay closed to settle within 0.01 %?
ask.explanation:
$C_H = Q_{inj}/\Delta V$ = {{Cmin|F}}, so $\tau = R_{ON}C_H$ = {{Ron*Cmin|s}}.
0.01 % needs $t = \tau\ln(10^4) \approx 9.2\tau$ = {{Ron*Cmin*ln(10000)|s}}. A smaller pedestal costs acquisition time.

steps.prompt: A relay coil ($L$ = {{L|H}}, {{I|A}}) on {{VDD|V}} is clamped by $D_1$ in series with a {{VZ|V}} Zener $D_Z$, to release faster than with a plain diode.

ask.prompt: Find the peak drain voltage of $Q_1$ at turn-off.
ask.explanation:
The coil current flows through $D_1$ (0.7 V) and the Zener in breakdown ($V_Z$) back to $V_{DD}$:
$V_D = V_{DD} + V_Z + 0.7$ = {{VDD|V}} + {{VZ|V}} + 0.7 V = {{VDD+VZ+0.7|V}}. Choose a MOSFET rated well above this.

ask.prompt: How long does the coil current take to fall to zero?
ask.explanation:
The coil sees a constant reverse voltage $V_Z + 0.7$ V, so the current ramps down linearly:
$t = \frac{LI}{V_Z + 0.7}$ = {{L|H}} × {{I|A}} / {{VZ+0.7|V}} = {{L*I/(VZ+0.7)|s}}. With only a diode (0.7 V) it would decay far more slowly.

steps.prompt: A p-channel MOSFET ($V_{GS(th)}$ = −2 V) is a high-side switch with its source on +12 V. How do you turn it **on**?
options: Pull the gate about 10 V below the source
steps.explanation: A p-channel enhancement MOSFET needs $V_{GS}$ well below its negative threshold: gate ≈ +2 V, so $V_{GS}$ ≈ −10 V. Gate at the source voltage ($V_{GS}$ = 0) turns it off. +17 V would be an n-channel high-side drive. A floating gate leaves it in an undefined state, so add a gate–source resistor.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for choosing a low-side MOSFET switch in order.
items: Find the supply voltage and load current
Check $R_{DS(on)}$ at the available gate drive
Check the junction temperature with the thermal resistance
steps.explanation: Start from the load (voltage, current, inductive or not), pick ratings with margin, then confirm the part is fully on at your gate voltage. Losses follow from $I^2R_{DS(on)}$ and the switching estimate, and the thermal resistance turns that loss into a temperature rise.
